topic.name: Surface Areas of Revolution: Rotation About the X-Axis

question.text: Consider the arc of the curve $x=\tan{y}$ that lies between $y=0$ and $y=\dfrac{\pi}{4}.$ What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis?
question.explanation:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

\[ S = \int 2\pi y\,\textrm d s. \]

Since we're given a curve in the form $x = f(y),$ we have

\[ \textrm d s = \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d y}\right)^2}\,\textrm d y. \] Therefore, we will use

\[ S = 2\pi \int_{y_1}^{y_2} y \sqrt{1+ \left( \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}y. \]

We are told that the limits of integration are from $y_1=0$ to $y_2=\dfrac{\pi}{4}.$

Computing the derivative, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y} ( \tan{y}) = \sec^2 {y}. \end{align*}

Finally, we obtain

\begin{align*} S &= 2\pi \int_{y_1}^{y_2} y \sqrt{1+ \left(\dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{0}^{\pi/4} y \sqrt{1+ \left(\sec^2{y}\right)^2} \: \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{0}^{\pi/4} y \sqrt{1+ \sec^4 {y}} \: \textrm{d}y . \\[5pt] \end{align*}

question.text: Consider the arc of the curve $x = \sin{y}$ that lies between $y = 0$ and $y=\dfrac{\pi}{3}.$ What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis?
question.explanation:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

\[ S = \int 2\pi y\,\textrm d s. \]

Since we're given a curve in the form $x = f(y),$ we have

\[ \textrm d s = \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d y}\right)^2}\,\textrm d y. \] Therefore, we will use

\[ S = 2\pi \int_{y_1}^{y_2} y \sqrt{1+ \left( \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}y. \]

We are told that the limits of integration are from $y_1=0$ to $y_2=\dfrac{\pi}{3}.$

Computing the derivative, we get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & = \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y} (\sin{y}) = \cos{y}. \end{align*}

Finally, we obtain \begin{align*} S & = 2\pi \int_{y_1}^{y_2} y \sqrt{1+ \left(\dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] & = 2\pi \int_{0}^{\pi/3} y \sqrt{1 + \cos^2{y}} \: \textrm{d}y . \end{align*}

example.title: Integrals Representing Surface Areas Generated by Functions of Y

question.text: Consider the arc of the curve $x=\sin{y}$ that lies in the first quadrant between its $y$-intercepts (see figure above). What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis?
question.explanation:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

\[ S = \int 2\pi y\,\textrm d s. \]

Since we're given a curve in the form $x = f(y),$ we have

\[ \textrm d s = \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d y}\right)^2}\,\textrm d y. \] Therefore, we will use

\[ S = 2\pi \int_{y_1}^{y_2} y \sqrt{1+ \left( \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}y. \]

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation:

\begin{align*} \sin{y} &= 0 \\[3pt] y &= \pm n\pi, \quad n \in \mathbb{Z} \end{align*}

Hence, we need to integrate from $y = 0$ to $y = \pi.$

Computing the derivative, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y} \left( \sin{y} \right) = \cos{y}. \end{align*}

Finally, we obtain

\begin{align*} S &= 2\pi \int_{y_1}^{y_2} y \sqrt{1+ \left(\dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] %&= 2\pi \int_{-\pi}^{0} y \sqrt{1+ \left(\cos{y}\right)^2} \: \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{0}^{\pi} y \sqrt{1+\cos^2{y}} \: \textrm{d}y . \\[5pt] \end{align*}

example.title: Integrals Representing Surface Areas Generated by Functions of Y

question.text: Consider the arc of the curve $y=\sqrt{4-x^2}$ that lies between the lines $x=-1$ and $x=1.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis.
question.explanation:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

\[ S = \int 2\pi y\,\textrm d s. \]

Since we're given a curve in the form $y = f(x),$ we have

\[ \textrm d s = \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}\right)^2}\,\textrm d x. \] Therefore, we will use

\[ S = 2\pi \int_{x_1}^{x_2} y \sqrt{1+ \left( \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}x. \]

We are told that the limits of integration are from $x_1=-1$ to $x_2=1.$

Computing the derivative, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x} (\sqrt {4-x^2} ) =-\dfrac{x}{\sqrt {4-x^2}} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \left(\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)^2 = \dfrac{x^2}{4-x^2}. \end{align*}

Therefore,

\begin{align*} S &= 2\pi \int_{x_1}^{x_2} y \sqrt{1+ \left( \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{-1}^{1} \sqrt{4-x^2} \sqrt{1+ \dfrac{x^2}{4-x^2}} \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{-1}^{1} \sqrt{4-x^2}\sqrt{\dfrac{4}{4-x^2}} \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] % &= 2\pi \int_{-1}^{1} \sqrt{4-x^2}\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{4-x^2}} \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{-1}^{1} 2 \: \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= 4\pi \big.x\,\big|_{-1}^1\\[5pt] &= 4\pi \left[ 1-(-1)\right]\\[5pt] &=8\pi. \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating a Surface Area of Revolution

question.text: Consider the arc of the curve $y=\sqrt{x}- \dfrac{1}{3}x^{3/2}$ that lies between the lines $x=0$ and $x=3.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis.
question.explanation:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

\[ S = \int 2\pi y\,\textrm d s. \]

Since we're given a curve in the form $y = f(x),$ we have

\[ \textrm d s = \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}\right)^2}\,\textrm d x. \] Therefore, we will use

\[ S = 2\pi \int_{x_1}^{x_2} y \sqrt{1+ \left( \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}x. \]

We are told that the limits of integration are from $x_1=0$ to $x_2=3.$

Computing the derivative, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x} \left(\sqrt{x}- \dfrac{1}{3}x^{3/2}\right) = \dfrac{1-x}{2\sqrt{x}} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \left(\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)^2 =\dfrac{1 - 2x + x^2}{4x}. \end{align*}

Therefore,

\begin{align*} S &= 2\pi \int_{x_1}^{x_2} y \sqrt{1+ \left( \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{0}^{3} \left(\sqrt{x}- \dfrac{1}{3}x^{3/2}\right) \sqrt{1+ \dfrac{1 - 2x + x^2}{4x}} \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{0}^{3} \left(\sqrt{x}- \dfrac{1}{3}x^{3/2}\right)\sqrt{\dfrac{(x+1)^2}{4x}} \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{0}^{3} \dfrac{\sqrt{x}\left(3- x\right)}{3}\left(\dfrac{x+1}{2\sqrt{x}}\right) \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\pi}{3} \int_{0}^{3} (3-x)(x+1)\: \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\pi}{3} \int_{0}^{3} ( 3+2x - x^2)\: \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi \left[ 3x + x^2 - \dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{0}^3\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\pi}{3} \cdot 9\\[5pt] &= 3\pi. \end{align*}
